title: Short Stuff: Scurvy
summary: Short Stuff episode on scurvy. The hosts explain that scurvy is a disease caused by long-term vitamin C deficiency, why humans (and other primates, guinea pigs, fruit bats) cannot synthesize vitamin C due to a non-functioning GULO gene, and how vitamin C supports collagen production. They describe symptoms (weakness, fatigue, weight loss, bleeding and swollen gums, tooth loss, joint pain, poor wound healing, brittle bones, and eventually fatal hemorrhage). They cover the history of scurvy among sailors, armies, and famines, with roughly two million naval deaths between 1500 and 1800, and James Lynn's 1747 controlled experiment showing citrus cured it. They note scurvy persists in poor and malnourished populations, that treatment with vitamin C works quickly, and close with the "Limey" nickname and a Civil War onion campaign poster.

segments.title: Opening banter and vitamin C basics
segments.summary: The hosts open the show and introduce scurvy as a disease from long-term lack of vitamin C. They joke about citrus and broccoli, which has about twice the vitamin C of an orange.

segments.title: Vitamin C synthesis in animals and humans
segments.summary: Most mammals can synthesize their own vitamin C, but humans, other primates, guinea pigs and fruit bats cannot. The hosts explain that humans have a non-functioning GULO gene, a mutation from evolutionary history. Vitamin C-rich foods like red peppers, potatoes, onions, tomatoes, and animal livers became important after humans migrated out of the tropics.

segments.title: Vitamin C, collagen and symptoms of scurvy
segments.summary: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, which supports bones, skin healing, and blood vessel walls. The hosts describe the stages of scurvy: faint weakness and fatigue, weight loss, bleeding and swollen gums, loose teeth, joint and muscle pain, poor wound healing, brittle bones, and eventually fatal hemorrhage in the brain or heart.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts say they will talk about pirates and sailors after a break.

segments.title: History of scurvy among sailors and armies
segments.summary: Scurvy was a problem for Crusader armies, during the Irish potato famine, and in the American Civil War. Between about 1500 and 1800 it was the leading cause of naval death, with around two million sailors dying, and surgeons sometimes cut away swollen gums. James Lynn's 1747 controlled experiment showed citrus could cure scurvy, though folk remedies like onions existed earlier.

segments.title: Modern scurvy and treatment
segments.summary: Scurvy persists today in poor and malnourished populations, including low-income families in the United States, and during famines. It is treatable: orange juice or vitamin C pills stop gum bleeding within 24 hours, with full recovery expected within about three months.

segments.title: Limeys, onion poster and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts mention that the British nickname limeys likely comes from the lime juice ration given to sailors, and a Civil War-era Chicago union poster urging soldiers to send an onion instead of a love letter. They sign off.
